dct_description_sm: This initial quantification of the June 2026 earthquake-induced debris across the most-affected Venezuelan states was derived through a multi-sensor synthetic aperture radar (SAR) change-detection analysis, integrated with rapid building damage assessments and supplemented by visual verification against very high-resolution optical imagery where available. Building footprints, including a modeled height attribute, were sourced from the Global Building Atlas [1] as the baseline layer, with locality-specific damage assessments and an independent SAR-derived damage product incorporated for areas where they were available, as detailed below. Damage to buildings was assessed through multiple sources and methods. A pixel-wise temporal t-test (PWTT) [2], adapted to a z-score formulation to accommodate the limited number of post-event Sentinel-1 acquisitions available at the time of analysis, was applied to Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) imagery, with buildings scoring above 0.4 retained for further assessment. This was complemented by damage assessment products from Copernicus EMS activation EMSR884 [3], as available on 27 June 2026, and by visual verification using PlanetScope imagery released through Planet's Crisis Response Program [4]. Building damage assessments produced by Microsoft's AI for Good Lab [5], generated by applying a classification model to post-event optical imagery acquired on 25 June 2026, were incorporated in their entirety for Catia La Mar, La Guaira, and Caraballeda. For locations with neither a locality-specific damage assessment nor high-resolution optical coverage, a Sentinel-1 SAR-based damage proxy map distributed via NASA's Disasters Program [6] was incorporated. This assessment estimates 96,046 buildings to have been damaged or destroyed., corresponding to nearly 3% of all buildings in the assessed states. For modeling purposes, minimum building height and average story height were considered to be 3m. Each built sq. meter is considered to have generated 1 tonne of debris. For visualization and modelling purposes, results were aggregated into a 7.8 sq. km hexagon grid. A substantial proportion of the debris remains within structurally compromised buildings and will only become accessible following demolition. [1] Zhu, X.X., Chen, S., Zhang, F., Shi, Y., & Wang, Y.
